conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the vascular surgery team. I understand you've been having some swelling in your neck and arms again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse over the last few days. It’s like the last time—swelling, headaches, blurry vision, especially when I lie back or lift my arms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds consistent with your SVC syndrome. We’re concerned the vein might be narrowing again. We’ll start with some imaging to check the blood flow in your neck veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they did an ultrasound. Is that what you’re planning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve ordered a limited neck ultrasound to look at your internal jugular veins. That’ll help us see if they’re open and flowing properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the ultrasound shows both your internal jugular veins are patent and compressible. No clots there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I still so swollen then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The blockage might be further down, in the superior vena cava itself. We’re planning a venogram tomorrow to get a detailed look at that area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they try to open it during the test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if we see a narrowing, we’ll attempt a venoplasty or stent placement. But we’ll know more once we see the images.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just worried it won’t work again, like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. We’ll do our best. In the meantime, we’re also checking on your Crohn’s symptoms—you mentioned nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been nauseous. I think my Crohn’s is flaring again. My stomach’s been tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI has been consulted. They’ll evaluate you and make sure we’re not missing an obstruction or ileus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to take you down for the venogram. It’s a procedure where we inject dye into your veins and take X-rays to see the blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember this from before. Is it safe with my allergies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your allergies, especially to iodine-based contrast. We’ll use a low-risk agent and monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well during the procedure. We found significant obstruction in your SVC, but unfortunately, the stent placement wasn’t successful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted cardiothoracic surgery. You may need an open surgical bypass. They’ll set up a future date for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds serious. Is it safe after all my other surgeries?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s complex, but they’ll evaluate your full history. For now, we’ll manage your symptoms and plan the next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also got your blood culture results back. One came back with coagulase-negative staph and Enterococcus faecium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that an infection? I’ve had line infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started you on IV antibiotics just in case, but you’ve been afebrile and your white count is normal. It’s likely a contaminant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re stopping the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discontinuing them. No need to treat if it’s not a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray to check your Crohn’s symptoms. The first one was hard to read, but today’s shows distended colon loops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like ileus—slowed bowel movement—common with Crohn’s flares. No surgical obstruction seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more treatment for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI cleared you. We’ll manage nausea with medication and let your bowel rest. Most improve with time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures showed no growth. Confirms the earlier result was likely contamination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were too, but you’re stable. Your neck swelling is still there, but not worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Crohn’s symptoms are a little better. Less nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep supporting you until discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? What about the SVC blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The venogram confirmed the obstruction, but we couldn’t fix it. Surgery is the next step—we’ll schedule that as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications? I was on a lot before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve simplified them. You’ll continue levothyroxine, citalopram, and pain meds as needed. We added Cipro in case your Crohn’s flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the contrast dye from the test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Drink plenty of fluids—about 2 liters today—to help flush it out. Avoid metformin for two days, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bandage at the procedure site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remove the pressure bandage tonight, use a clean band-aid. Keep it dry—no showering for now. Watch for bruising or lumps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go up and down stairs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Limit stair climbing today. No lifting over 10 pounds for three days. Rest as much as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see cardiothoracic surgery to plan the bypass. GI follow-up in a few weeks. Call us if swelling worsens or you develop fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better knowing what’s next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. Take care, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.
